opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the older algorithm, attribution-based parameter decomposition, or APD, tried to decompose the network's parameters directly into a set of parameter components, where each component was a full vector in parameter space spanning all the layers. Each one was supposed to correspond to a mechanism the network uses. We wanted those components to sum to the original parameters, to be as simple as possible, and to have as few of them active on any given input as possible.

The trouble was that this was hard to optimize. You had to pick in advance how many components to use. Each component was a huge object, the same size as the whole network. You had to choose which components were active using a top-k step over attributions, which was finicky and sensitive to hyperparameters. And you were trying to get both simplicity and minimality from the same object, which made things awkward.

With stochastic parameter decomposition, SPD, we break that up. Instead of whole-network components, we decompose each weight matrix into a sum of rank-one subcomponents, outer products of a vector in the input space and a vector in the output space. These are the atoms. I think of an APD-style parameter component, a full mechanism, as roughly a cluster of these rank-one subcomponents, possibly across several layers and matrices, that tend to be used together. So SPD works at a finer level, and you can rebuild the bigger mechanism-level components by grouping subcomponents that co-activate or depend on each other causally.

Making everything rank-one gets you a lot of the simplicity pressure for free. You no longer need a separate penalty pushing components toward low rank, because each subcomponent is already as simple as it can be in that sense. And the subcomponents are cheap, so you can have lots of them per layer.

The other big change is how we decide what's active. APD used gradient attributions and a top-k cutoff. In SPD we learn a causal importance for each subcomponent on each input, predicted by small auxiliary networks. Then during training we randomly ablate subcomponents in proportion to how unimportant they're predicted to be, and require the network's output to stay the same. That stochastic masking gives a much cleaner signal about whether a subcomponent actually matters causally on a given datapoint, instead of relying on a linear approximation from gradients.

So, in short: the APD parameter component and the SPD rank-one subcomponent are aiming at the same thing, a decomposition of the parameters into the mechanisms the network uses. SPD just moves the basic unit down to something smaller and easier to optimize, and treats full mechanisms as structure that appears when you group those units. In practice that's been much more stable and scalable, and it removes a lot of the hyperparameter sensitivity that made APD painful.

r001.rationale: The response defines each subcomponent as an outer product of input- and output-space vectors, but it does not explain that the matrix maps activation along one read direction into one write direction.

r002.rationale: It says an APD-style parameter component can be understood as a cluster of SPD rank-one subcomponents, grouped across layers and matrices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the simplest way to put it is that the rank-one subcomponents are the atoms, and the parameter components from the older approach, APD, are the molecules you can build out of them.

In attribution-based parameter decomposition, we were trying to learn a fixed set of parameter components directly. Each one was a full-rank-capable chunk of parameters that lived in the same space as the network's weights, and we asked them to sum to the original weights while being faithful, minimal, and simple. The problem was that we had to decide up front how many components there were and we had to learn the rank of each one as part of the optimization. That turned out to be fragile. You'd get components that were too high-rank, or you'd get things that shattered mechanisms into pieces, and the hyperparameters were really unforgiving.

Stochastic parameter decomposition takes a step back and says, let's not learn components with learned rank. Let's instead decompose each weight matrix into a bunch of rank-one pieces, an outer product of two vectors, and have way more of them than we think we need. Then each one gets a causal importance, a scalar between zero and one that says how much this particular rank-one piece matters for the network's output on this particular input. The stochastic part is that during training we randomly ablate subcomponents in proportion to how unimportant they're predicted to be, and we require the network to still produce the right output. That's what pushes the model to use as few subcomponents as it can per input, which is the minimality idea from APD, but implemented in a way that's much better behaved.

So where does the old notion of a parameter component go? It becomes an emergent object rather than a thing you parameterize directly. If you look at which rank-one subcomponents tend to be causally important together, across inputs, they cluster. A mechanism that genuinely needs a rank-three direction in some layer will show up as three rank-one subcomponents that fire together. That cluster is what APD would have called a single parameter component. We're just not forcing the decomposition to commit to that grouping ahead of time, we let the data tell us.

The nice thing about this is that it dissolves a lot of the issues we had. You don't need to guess the number of components. The rank of each mechanism comes for free from how many atoms co-activate. And because every subcomponent is rank-one, the optimization landscape is much smoother, so it scales to models where APD just wouldn't train. The cost is that you lose a little of the conceptual cleanliness, because a "component" is now something you read off after the fact rather than a first-class object in the loss. But honestly, I think that's the right trade. The old framing was asking the optimizer to solve a clustering problem and a decomposition problem at the same time, and separating those two turned out to be most of the win.

r001.rationale: The response describes each subcomponent as an outer product of two vectors, but does not explain that it maps activation along a read direction into a write direction.

r002.rationale: It says rank-one subcomponents are “atoms” that can be grouped into emergent parameter components, which correspond to components in the older APD approach.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two different levels of granularity. In the older algorithm, a component could contain a fairly general update to the model’s parameter matrices. In stochastic parameter decomposition, the basic building blocks are rank-one pieces. So the closer analogue of an old component would be a collection of those rank-one pieces that work together to implement some behavior, rather than necessarily a single rank-one piece.

That distinction matters because the unit we use to parameterize the decomposition doesn’t have to be the unit we ultimately want to interpret. Rank-one pieces give us a finer-grained way to break the parameters apart; then the question is how those pieces compose into meaningful computational structures.

r001.rationale: It describes rank-one pieces as finer-grained building blocks but does not explain that a rank-one parameter matrix maps activation from a single read direction to a single write direction.

r002.rationale: It says an older component is more closely analogous to a collection of rank-one pieces that work together, clearly describing how the subcomponents can be grouped into older-algorithm components.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the rank-one subcomponents are a finer-grained building block. In the older algorithm, a parameter component could contain a higher-rank update to a weight matrix, and could have parameters spread across multiple layers. So it was a more flexible object.

In stochastic parameter decomposition, you break things down into rank-one pieces, and then the question is which of those pieces need to be used together. A collection of rank-one subcomponents could therefore play the role of one of those larger parameter components. But I wouldn’t assume there’s a clean one-to-one correspondence between what the two methods learn. Changing the granularity and the optimization changes which decomposition you end up finding.
